The agent mesh, plus the overnight hardening pass on it.

Five defects were found and fixed by attacking it rather than reading it, two
of them P0:

- A terminal execution record could be resurrected. "Latest" was decided by a
  wall-clock stamp, so two writes in one millisecond were unordered and the
  guard compared against the older record; the terminal state was lost.
- A compute budget could roll back to less spend. Same mistake, but the state
  is money: 700 cents committed loaded back as 0 committed and full capacity
  available.
- Safe retry did not exist: a reservation released without spending anything
  permanently blocked its own task.
- A task declaring no consequence class was accepted and reserved compute;
  unknown consequential state now fails closed.
- A crash-recovery replay was rejected because its keys arrived in a different
  order.

Three of those were one error in three files -- "latest" meaning most recently
stamped rather than furthest along a monotonic quantity. All five sites with
that shape are now resolved: three fixed, two proven safe with the reason
recorded.

the wiring made those run twice and inflated the count. Reverted, and the
build-wiring guard now follows the import graph and catches double-listing in
both directions.

Every fix verified by reverting it and confirming the matching test fails.
Two adversarial sweeps with different mental models found no new P0/P1, and
both are kept as tests/agent-mesh-adversarial-sweep.test.mjs.

Keep the adversarial sweeps as tests, and close the matrix

Two sweeps were run against the guards added this session, with deliberately
different mental models: a malicious model sending hostile payloads, then a
hostile scheduler against a stale store.

Sweep 1 produced two findings and neither was a defect. One was my own probe
using an incomplete task fixture, so every case in that block failed for
valid-claimed-relay-task-required rather than for the reason I was testing.
The other is that reserveCompute coerces a numeric string -- "10" becomes 10 --
which is lenient but still passes isSafeInteger and every budget bound, so no
capacity can be created. Both are recorded in the matrix as accepted behaviour
rather than quietly dropped, because a finding that turns out to be nothing is
still worth being able to look up.

Sweep 2 found nothing. It attacked specifically the new guards: a stale write
arriving later in the log, two different terminal statuses at one instant, a
budget tie where only tokens moved (the cost tiebreak cannot carry that one),
four shapes of sequence rewind including NaN and absent, and every
reserve/release/commit interleaving.

Both sweeps now live in tests/agent-mesh-adversarial-sweep.test.mjs rather than
a scratch directory. An attack that only ran once is a story; an attack that
runs on every commit is a guard.

The failure matrix is closed out. All five sites with the ordering pattern are

Close the last two ordering gaps: autonomy run state is now protected, not just ordered

The previous report listed these as known-open. They are the fourth and fifth
instance of one mistake, and the pattern is now fully swept.

P1: listLatestAutonomyRuns deduplicated per run with `rowTime > currentTime` --
strictly greater, so a timestamp tie kept the FIRST row seen, which is the
older snapshot. That is not cosmetic: agent-autonomy-job reads this listing to
choose which runs to sweep, so a stale status can put a finished run back into
the active set and have its work redone.

P2 (previously recorded as an open gap): saveAutonomyRunSnapshot enforced no
transition guard at all. Any snapshot was accepted, including one that moved a
run backwards. Run state was ordered but not protected.

Both are closed with the run's own `sequence`, which the pump only ever
increments, so it is a real monotonic authority rather than a guess:

  - a lower sequence is refused as autonomy-run-sequence-regression
  - the same sequence with identical content is an idempotent crash replay
  - the same sequence with different content is autonomy-run-snapshot-conflict,
    because two writers disagreeing about one point in a run must not be
    silently appended
  - loading and listing both rank on sequence first

One existing test had to change. It saved two different run states at the same
sequence by hand and relied on the later one silently overwriting the earlier.
The real pump never produces that -- every advancing path goes through
`next.sequence += 1` -- so the fixture was corrected to advance the sequence,
which preserves what the test was actually checking (the listing dedups to the
latest) while matching how the system behaves. No gate was weakened; a gate was
added, and the new conflict case is now covered explicitly.

The two remaining sites from the previous report were reviewed and are safe,
with the reason recorded rather than assumed:

  - agent-code-artifact-store rejects any digest divergence as
    artifact-identity-collision BEFORE the sort, so every candidate row is
    byte-identical content and the tie only affects provenance metadata.
  - listCloudRelayTasks feeds display only; no authority decision reads it.

Full gate: check:syntax passes, 1388 tests, 1346 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped,
npm audit 0 vulnerabilities. Both fixes verified by reverting them and watching
the matching test fail.

Undo my double-counting, and fix the guard that caused it

I reported that 171 mesh tests "had never executed" and wired 23 files into
test:deterministic to fix it. That was wrong, and the wiring made things worse.

tests/agent-relay.test.mjs imports 19 of those suites, and that file is in
test:deterministic. They were running all along. Naming them as well made them
execute twice, which is why the suite jumped to 1521 -- a number that looked
like progress and was double-counting. Verified by name: the same test titles
appeared twice in the output.

Root cause is my own build-wiring guard. It counted package.json references
only, so any file that runs by import looked orphaned. A verification tool
that is wrong is worse than no tool, because it manufactures confident action
-- which is precisely what it did to me.

Fixed properly:

  - The orphan check now resolves the import graph transitively. A test file
    runs if a script names it OR if something that runs imports it.
  - A second guard catches the inverse mistake: a file both named by a script
    and imported by another script's file executes twice, inflating the pass
    count that a reader trusts and doubling runtime for nothing.
  - The 19 double-listed files are removed from the script. The importing file
    already runs them.

Both directions were checked by deliberately reintroducing each fault: adding
agent-worker-runtime.test.mjs back to the script fails the double-listing
guard by name, and dropping an unreferenced file into tests/ fails the orphan
guard by name.

Verified position: zero test files are orphaned, and none run twice.

The check:syntax additions from that commit stay. node --check does not follow
imports, so covering 25 previously unchecked src modules -- including
security.mjs and crypto.mjs -- was real and is unaffected by this.

Honest numbers now: 1386 tests, 1344 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped. The earlier
1521 was inflated. The report and failure matrix are corrected in this commit
rather than left to read as achievement.

Stop a compute budget rolling back to less spend when snapshot timestamps collide

P0, and the same shape as the execution-record resurrection fixed in the
previous commit -- except the state being rewound here is money.

loadLatestComputeBudget picked the newest snapshot by sorting on wall-clock
alone. Two saves for one budget inside the same millisecond are
indistinguishable to that sort, so the loader could restore an OLDER budget:
less spend recorded, more capacity free.

Measured deterministically by stamping three snapshots with one fixed instant:

  true state : 700 cents committed, 300 available
  loaded     : 0 cents committed, 1000 available

Seven hundred cents of recorded spend vanished and the same capacity
reappeared from nowhere -- on restart, after a crash, exactly when the system
is least able to notice. The value-level conservation property was already
tested and held; nothing tested conservation across persistence, which is
where it actually broke.

committedCostCents and committedTokens only ever increase: commit adds to
them, and neither reserve nor release touches them. So they are a monotonic
ordering key. Snapshots now rank by recorded spend first, then time, then the
store's row sequence, and the newest wins regardless of what the clock says.

Finding this immediately after the execution-record bug is the useful part.
Both were the same mistake in different files: "latest" defined as "most
recently stamped" rather than "furthest along a monotonic quantity". The
remaining time-only sorts in agent-autonomy-store, agent-code-artifact-store
and cloud-agent-relay have the same shape and are recorded in the failure
matrix as unreviewed rather than quietly assumed safe.

Pin authority attenuation across autonomous child tasks

Stop a terminal execution being resurrected by two writes in the same millisecond

P0, found by the soak rather than by reading the state machine.

"Latest execution record" was decided by sorting on detail.createdAt, which is
a wall-clock stamp. Two writes for one task inside the same millisecond -- a
fast worker, or any clock coarser than the gap between two saves -- are
indistinguishable to that sort, so the transition guard could compare a new
write against the OLDER record instead of the newest.

Measured, deterministically, by passing one fixed date to three saves:

  MODEL_RESULT_READY   -> saved
  RESULT_SUBMITTED     -> saved
  MODEL_RESULT_READY   -> ACCEPTED, terminal task reopened
  loadLatestAgentExecution -> MODEL_RESULT_READY

The terminal state was not merely bypassed, it was lost. Every guard in
validateExecutionTransition was correct and none of them ran against the right
record.

Ordering now ranks by how far along the state machine a record is, then by
time, then by the store's own row sequence. That puts the monotonicity
invariant into the ordering itself, so a terminal record wins over an earlier
stage whatever the clock says -- which also covers skew, rollback, and
out-of-order delivery, none of which a timestamp sort survives. The sequence
tiebreak compares the numeric tail of the row id, because "row-9" sorts after
"row-12" lexically.

Also adds tests/agent-mesh-soak.test.mjs: 1,000 tasks through the real state
machines with crashes injected at four durable boundaries (before dispatch,
after model success before persistence, after persistence before submission,
after submission before recording it), plus a concurrency race and a direct
resurrection attempt. It asserts each boundary was actually exercised -- a
soak that never crashed proves nothing about crash recovery -- and checks
capacity conservation, no duplicate compute, no lost terminal state, and
bounded audit growth.

That soak is what found this. Reverting the ordering fix fails soak tests 1
and 3; restored, 3/3.

Fail closed when a task declares no consequence class at all

The worker is only permitted to do local preparation, and it checked for that
like this:

  if (task.consequenceClass && task.consequenceClass !== 'LOCAL_PREPARATION')

The guard fires only when a class is PRESENT and wrong. A task that declares
nothing skips the check entirely and is accepted. Measured before fixing: a
task with no consequenceClass reached READY_TO_EXECUTE and went on to reserve
compute.

Silence is not consent. An undeclared consequence class is unknown
consequential state, and the whole point of this boundary is that unknown
fails closed. The two problems also deserve different reasons: "you asked for
something I am not allowed to do" and "you did not say what you are asking
for" send a reader to different places.

Nothing in the repository actually relied on the hole -- the canonical task
compiler always declares a class -- so closing it changed no existing
behaviour. The full suite is unchanged at 0 failures.

One of the new tests covers a property the fix could have missed: a refused
task must reserve no compute. Failing closed after the reservation would let a
stream of undeclared tasks drain the budget while being rejected.

Verified by reverting: 3 of 5 tests fail, including the empty-string and
no-compute-held cases. Restored: 5/5.

Stop rejecting a crash-recovery replay because its keys arrived in a different order

Terminal idempotency exists so that a crash after the work is done converges
instead of conflicting. The record that comes back on recovery is rebuilt from
persisted pieces, so its fields arrive in whatever order the rebuilding code
emits them -- not necessarily the order they were first written in.

sameExecutionRecord compared with a raw JSON.stringify, which makes key order
part of the identity. Measured: an execution record replayed with identical
facts and reordered keys returned terminal-execution-history-conflict. The
guard rejected the replay on exactly the path it exists to serve.

This branch already had the right answer twenty lines away, in
cloud-agent-relay's canonicalValue/sameJson, written for the same problem in
the relay. Two implementations of "are these the same record" is how one of
them ends up order-sensitive while the other is not, so sameJson is now
exported and reused rather than copied. One canonical primitive.

The comparison is order-insensitive for object keys only. Arrays are left
alone deliberately -- [a,b] and [b,a] are different data, and collapsing them
would hide a real divergence. There is a test for that, alongside tests that a
different provider and different usage numbers are still conflicts. Making a
comparison forgiving must not make it blind.

3/4 pass. Restored: 4/4.

Let a safely-released compute task try again, and prove capacity is conserved

Found by attacking the budget rather than reading it.

P1: a released reservation permanently blocked its own retry. reserveCompute
refused any taskId present in the reservation map, which lumps together three
situations that need different answers:

  RESERVED  -- live. Reserving again lets two workers spend one allocation.
  COMMITTED -- compute was already bought under this identity. Reserving again
               is how you pay twice for one task.
  RELEASED  -- capacity handed back, NO provider call made (rate limited,
               cancelled before dispatch). Nothing to double-spend.

Only the first two are double-spend risks. Refusing the third strands the task
forever: the budget reports full capacity and that task can never touch it, so
the safe-retry path -- the one for failures known not to have executed -- did
not exist. Measured before fixing: reserve, release, retry -> refused, with
1000/1000 cents available.

Now RELEASED may be re-reserved and the earlier attempt is carried forward as
attempt/priorReservationIds rather than overwritten, so the history stays
readable. RESERVED and COMMITTED are refused exactly as before, and there are
tests for both -- loosening one status must not loosen the others.

P2: the reservation cap reported 'reservation-count-limit-reached' whether the
map was full of live reservations or of finished history. Those need opposite
responses from an operator. Terminal records still count toward the bound,
because the map is the audit trail and unbounded growth is a real memory
concern, but the reason code now says which limit was reached.

tests/ai-compute-budget-conservation.test.mjs attacks the invariant that
matters: capacity can be spent, returned, or held, never created. A seeded
3,000-step random walk of reserve/commit/release checks the invariant after
every transition, not just at the end -- a budget that goes briefly wrong and
recovers is still wrong. It asserts the run actually exercised release (>50)
and retry-after-release (>10), because a property test that never reaches the
path it exists for proves nothing.

Verified by reverting the fix: 3 of the 6 new tests fail, including the
conservation walk. Restored: 6/6.

Fix the HTTP ingress: poll was broken, and receipts lost their provenance

The ingress had never handled a real request. Every test drove it with a fake
client, so nothing had ever exercised the code that builds GitHub URLs or
forwards a submit. Running it once against the real API found two defects.

poll returned 400. The transport passes state 'OPEN'; GitHub answers 422 for
anything but lowercase. The operation ChatGPT uses to discover work at all was
broken against the real API while the unit suite was green -- because every
fake accepted whatever it was handed. Normalised at the client boundary, which
is the layer that has to speak GitHub's dialect, rather than asking each
caller to remember.

Receipt provenance was discarded in silence. Only workerId, status and result
were forwarded, so a caller that carefully supplied sourceCommit, confidence,
findings, limitations and duration got a receipt recording UNKNOWN for all of
them -- and a 200 RECEIVED saying it had worked. Dropping evidence while
reporting success is the worst failure this contract can have. Issue #65
captures it; #66 is the same request afterwards, with every field intact.

The tests now drive the real client through a fake fetch, and the fake behaves
like GitHub instead of accepting anything: it returns 422 for a non-lowercase
state, exactly as the API does. A fake that says yes to everything is not a
test double, it is a way to keep a bug.

One of the new tests exists for a failure mode worse than the 400 -- a
validation error that turns into 200 with count:0, which reads as "no work to
do" when the truth is "the query was rejected". It pins that this fails loudly.

Both regression tests were verified by reverting each fix in turn and
confirming the matching test fails. A test that cannot fail is not protection.

1195 tests, 1153 pass, 0 fail, 42 skipped. 13/13 in vercel-agent-relay.

The ingress is still deployed nowhere. This was driven over loopback against
the real GitHub API, which exercises every line except the hosting.

Stop the worker reporting a killed suite as a failure, or a lost result as work done

Two defects, both of the same kind: a failure shaped like a success.

A timed-out suite was reported as a failed one. execFile signals a timeout
kill the same way it signals a non-zero exit, and nothing separated them, so
a suite that never finished produced status FAILED, confidence HIGH,
truthTable FAILED and decision REPAIR. Captured on issue #61: that receipt
asserts the deterministic suite fails. It does not -- it passes 1191 tests.
The receipt claimed a verification result it never obtained, at high
confidence, and asked a reviewer to repair something that is fine. A timeout
now reports NOT_RUN, LOW confidence, OWNER_REQUIRED, and a limitation saying
in plain words that this is not evidence the suite fails.

The first attempt at that fix did not work, and issue #61 is the record of
it. The check tested `error.code === undefined`; Node sets it to `null` on a
timeout kill, so the condition silently never matched and the bug shipped
looking fixed. `killed === true` is the marker. Verified against the real
error object rather than assumed a second time.

A failed submit counted as handled work. `handled += 1` ran unconditionally,
so a result that could not be filed consumed a slot against maxTasks -- the
worker stopped early having accomplished nothing -- and logged at normal
level as though the task were done. What actually follows is the lease
lapsing, the task stranding, and one of its three attempts spent on work that
was completed and thrown away. It now logs SUBMIT FAILED at error level,
counts nothing, and exits non-zero so a scheduler notices instead of
recording a clean run.

Also corrected a claim I made when proposing this work: a stale poll snapshot
is NOT a bug. claimGithubRelayTask re-reads the issue and its comments and
refuses with task-already-completed, so the claim is the authority and the
snapshot cannot cause duplicate work. Checked before building anything.

Proved live: #61 the old behaviour, #62 the corrected timeout receipt, #63 a
forced submit failure exiting 1 with "handled 0 task(s), 1 submit failure(s)".

Renew the lease while a suite runs, and stop when it is gone (#60)

The worker never heartbeated. A suite outlasting its lease would finish, try
to submit, and be refused -- work discarded with no message anyone would look
for. It fit today only because check:syntax takes 16s against a 1800s lease.

Renews once a minute (RELAY_HEARTBEAT_MS) and kills the child if a renewal is
refused. A transient network error is not treated as a lost lease; only an
explicit refusal is.

Both branches proved live. Renewal: 5 renewals across a 2-minute suite (#57).
Abort: a rival submitting mid-run was REFUSED because heartbeating keeps the
lease alive (#58), making the obvious test unreachable -- so the state was
forced by writing the result comment directly, and the worker detected
task-already-completed, killed the child and submitted nothing (#59).

Also recorded: GitHub's label index lags issue creation, so a freshly created
task can poll as invisible. Not a defect, but it looks exactly like a parse
failure and is not one.

Renew the lease while a suite runs, and stop when it is gone
